Pantry Guide · February 28, 2024 · 12 min read

24 pantry staples that make weeknight cooking actually work

Build this list once. Shop the gaps. Spend the rest of the year cooking better dinners with less panic.

A well-stocked pantry isn't about having everything. It's about having the right twenty-something things — the ones that quietly unlock dozens of meals. Most overstuffed pantries are full of single-use ingredients bought for one recipe and never touched again. That's not a pantry; that's a graveyard. The goal is a small, deep set of staples you reach for constantly.

Here's the philosophy we cook by: buy the pantry once, or build it gradually over a few trips, and then every week you only shop for fresh ingredients. The base is already home. This single shift cuts both your grocery bill and your decision fatigue, because the hardest part of any weeknight dinner — "what do I even have to work with?" — is already answered before you start.

It's also the foundation of everything we do at Northstar Pantry. Every recipe we build assumes this base is in your cupboard. If your pantry has these items, the shopping list we send you each week is shorter, cheaper, and faster to shop. So consider this the prerequisite — build it once, and every plan after gets easier.

Below are 24 staples in five categories, with the specific type to buy and why it earns its shelf space.

Category 1 Canned & Jarred

The backbone of fast dinners. These don't spoil, they don't judge you, and they turn a bare fridge into a meal.

  • 01Crushed San Marzano tomatoes (28 oz, DOP certified) The difference between okay pasta and great pasta is the tomato. San Marzanos are sweeter and less acidic. Spend the extra dollar.
  • 02White beans (cannellini, 3–4 cans) The most versatile bean. Pasta e fagioli, white bean soup, smashed with garlic and olive oil as a side. Keep four cans.
  • 03Chickpeas (3 cans) Roast them crispy for salads, simmer in tomato sauce for shakshuka, blend into hummus. Buy the no-salt-added kind.
  • 04Coconut milk (full fat, 2 cans) Not just for Thai food. Adds richness to soups, braises, and even oatmeal. Full fat or don't bother.
  • 05Fish sauce (Red Boat or Tiparos) Don't be afraid of it. A teaspoon in a pan sauce or braise adds a savory depth that tastes like you cooked all day.
  • 06Dijon mustard A tablespoon into any pan sauce makes it taste finished. Also the base of the world's best vinaigrette.

Category 2 Oils, Vinegars & Acid

Fat carries flavor; acid wakes it up. Get these right and almost everything you cook tastes more alive.

  • 07Good olive oil (everyday + finishing) Two bottles: one decent workhorse for cooking, one nicer one for finishing dishes and salads. Kirkland extra-virgin is genuinely excellent for an everyday bottle.
  • 08Sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar More complex than white wine vinegar, less harsh than apple cider. Brightens everything.
  • 09Soy sauce or tamari Tamari is gluten-free and slightly richer. A splash in braises, stir-fries, or even roast chicken glazes.
  • 10Lemons (always fresh) Not a pantry item technically, but always buy four. A squeeze of lemon at the end of any dish is the most underused trick in home cooking.

"A well-stocked pantry isn't about abundance — it's about the right 24 things that unlock a hundred dinners."

— Northstar Pantry kitchen team

Category 3 Dry Goods & Grains

These are the part of the plate that makes a meal feel like dinner instead of a snack. They keep for months and stretch a little protein a long way.

  • 11Pasta (two shapes: a long and a short) Keep spaghetti and rigatoni. Long pasta for simple sauces, short pasta for chunkier sauces and soups.
  • 12Pearl barley Underappreciated. Nutty, chewy, filling. Goes into soups, stews, grain bowls. Cooks in 30 minutes.
  • 13Farro More character than brown rice, faster to cook. Great base for weeknight grain bowls.
  • 14Panko breadcrumbs For crisping, binding, and topping. Regular breadcrumbs are fine but panko stays crunchier.
  • 15All-purpose flour (and a small bag of 00 pizza flour) 00 flour makes noticeably better pizza and pasta. Worth having a small bag around.
  • 16Dried red lentils Cook in 20 minutes with no soaking. Make soup, dal, or blend into a sauce base.

Category 4 Spices That Actually Matter

Don't try to own every spice. Own these five deeply. A full spice cabinet you never use is worse than a small one you know well — those forgotten jars lose their punch and take up the room your real workhorses need.

  • 17Smoked paprika The flavor backbone of a dozen dinners: chicken thighs, chickpeas, fish, eggs. Buy Spanish, not generic.
  • 18Cumin (whole and ground) Toast whole seeds in a dry pan to understand why it matters. Ground cumin for quick weeknights.
  • 19Coriander (ground) Works alongside cumin in almost everything. Floral and citrusy when fresh.
  • 20Dried chili flakes Calabrian chili paste if you can find it. Regular red pepper flakes otherwise. Heat and flavor, not just heat.
  • 21Turmeric Anti-inflammatory, yes, but also: it makes everything golden and beautiful. Into soups, rice, eggs.

Category 5 Alliums & Flavor Base

Technically the produce aisle, but they live in the pantry and they start nearly every dinner you'll make. Never run out.

  • 22Yellow onions (always have 4–6) The foundation of 80% of dinners. Always have too many.
  • 23Garlic (whole bulbs, not pre-minced) Pre-minced garlic in a jar is a lie. Buy whole heads and mince fresh. The difference is real.
  • 24Shallots Subtler than onions, slightly sweeter. Essential for pan sauces and vinaigrettes. Keep 4–6 around.

That's the whole list. Twenty-four things, five trips to put together if you spread it out, and a kitchen that's ready for almost anything after that. You'll notice none of it is exotic — that's the point. The magic isn't in any single ingredient; it's in always having the base on hand so the only question left is what's fresh this week.

If you want to see how these staples become actual dinners, take a look at this week's menu — every recipe is built with this list as the foundation, so the shopping list is short and the cooking is calm.

Make it real

Your pantry starter checklist

Print this, shop it over two or three trips, and you're set for the rest of the year.

Canned & Jarred

  • San Marzano tomatoes (28 oz)
  • Cannellini beans (3–4 cans)
  • Chickpeas (3 cans)
  • Full-fat coconut milk (2 cans)
  • Fish sauce
  • Dijon mustard

Oils, Vinegars & Acid

  • Olive oil (everyday + finishing)
  • Sherry or red wine vinegar
  • Soy sauce or tamari
  • Lemons (always four)

Dry Goods & Grains

  • Pasta (one long, one short)
  • Pearl barley
  • Farro
  • Panko breadcrumbs
  • Flour (AP + small bag 00)
  • Dried red lentils

Spices & Alliums

  • Smoked paprika (Spanish)
  • Cumin (whole + ground)
  • Ground coriander
  • Dried chili flakes
  • Turmeric
  • Yellow onions (4–6)
  • Garlic (whole bulbs)
  • Shallots (4–6)
